fields.meaning: In the middle of… / during…
examples: We're in a meeting right now.
You must not use your smartphone during class.
In Japan, cherry blossoms bloom from March through April.
It was raining all day long.
People all over the world are paying attention.
fields.explain:
N + ちゅう : Used for a state in progress → “in the middle of…”.
Example:使用中（in use）,勉強中（studying）.
N + じゅう : Indicates the whole scope → “throughout…”, “all over…”.
Example:一年中（all year round）,日本中（all over Japan）.
When it is hard to tell them apart, you can rely on the meaning of the sentence or the dictionary reading.

•
① In the middle of…（～しているところ）：expresses an action or state in progress.
“While…”, “in the middle of…”.

•
② The whole / throughout / all over…（～の全体）：expresses the whole scope of time/space.
“Throughout…”, “all over…”.

•
Pronunciation:

・Depending on the word it attaches to, it is read ちゅう or じゅう.
・N + ちゅう：in progress (授業中, 使用中, 会議中).
・N + じゅう：throughout, the whole scope (一日中, 世界中, 年中).
fields.notes:
• Besides the common readings, some special cases must be memorized word by word.
• Do not use the particle に before 中 when it means “in the middle of…” (✕ 授業に中 → ○ 授業中).
• It can follow quantities: 5分 中（within 5 minutes）, 3回 中2回（2 out of 3 times）.
mistakes: Confusing “ちゅう” and “じゅう” → decide by the meaning of the word: a state (ちゅう) or the whole scope (じゅう).
Confusing it with ～の間 (during a period of time) → 間 emphasizes a stretch of time, 中 emphasizes a state in progress.
The JLPT often tests the correct reading and the difference in nuance: 会議中 vs 一日中.

fields.meaning: When/in case of ~
examples: In case of fire or earthquake, please do not use the elevator.

A: What should I do if I'm in a traffic accident?
B: Please contact the police right away.

A: Um, what should I do if I want a receipt?
B: If you need one, please tell the store staff.
fields.explain:
Supposes a certain situation; the part that follows is how to deal with it or the result that occurs.
Since 場合 is a noun, the formation is the same as for modifiers of a noun.
fields.notes:
Used when picking out just one of various situations that could occur and addressing it. ①～⑥ can be rephrased with 「…時は」. However, 「場合」 cannot be used in sentences that express a concrete time relationship based on the speaker's personal experience, as below.
*(correct) 私が行った時には会議は始まっていた。
*(incorrect) 私が行った場合には会議は始まっていた。

fields.name: ～volitional form＋と思う
fields.meaning: stating one's own intention or plan (similar to つもり）
examples: After graduating, I'm thinking of getting a job instead of continuing my studies.
I think I'll take it easy and rest at home this weekend.
“What are you planning to do over winter break?” “I'm thinking of going back to my country.”
I meant to get up at 7, but I went to bed late last night, so I couldn't get up.
fields.notes:
Note:
●主語が三人称のときは「～（よ）うと思います」は使えない。
When the subject is third person, 「と思います」 cannot be used.
1.  〇　わたしは彼女と結婚しようと思います。
I'm thinking of marrying her.
2.  〇　わたしは彼女と結婚しようと思っています。
I'm thinking of marrying her.
3.  X山田さんは彼女と結婚しようと思います。
Yamada is thinking of marrying her.
4.  〇山田さんは彼女と結婚しようと思っています。
Yamada is thinking of marrying her.

fields.meaning: Expresses the speaker's volition. The subject of the sentence is first person. The pattern おもっています is used to express the speaker's continuing volition, as in examples ②③④. The pattern ～とはおもいません expresses a strong negation, as in example ⑤.
fields.connection: V volitional form + と思います
examples: The weather is nice, so I think I'll go out.
I'm going on a trip, so I'm thinking of buying a bag.
I'm thinking of stopping by the library on my way home today.
I'm thinking of traveling around Europe next year.
I wouldn't think of going to karaoke alone.

fields.name: ～（ら）れます（ability）
fields.meaning: Expresses an ability to do something (①②) or a situation in which an action can be done and is always available (③). It can also express a possibility as a property of a thing, as in example ④. Used with volitional verbs expressing human actions. Often the particle
fields.connection: V potential form (話せます・食べられます)
examples: Joe can speak English, Japanese, and Chinese.
Hana still can't get dressed by herself.
You can see famous paintings at this art museum.
This water is not drinkable.
Would you like coffee? Or would you prefer tea?
Are we eating at home tonight, or eating out?
Shall we go with this plan, or choose a different one?
I don't know whether he will come or not.
Train? Or bus?
Shall we speak in English? Or would Japanese be better?
fields.explain:
Used when presenting 2 (sometimes 3) mutually exclusive options; not used for open-ended listing.
Usually stands between two interrogative clauses, or after a short question to add another option.
Natural in conversation; in documents/forms it is usually replaced by または／あるいは／もしくは.
In indirect questions: Aか、 それとも Bか… presents two possibilities and is followed by a 動詞 such as 決める・迷う・分からない.
Intonation: put light stress on それとも to make the “or” clear.

• Connects two mutually exclusive options in a question: “A or B?”.
• Expects the listener to choose one option; the intonation rises at the end of the sentence in a question.
• Typical of conversation, neutral in formality (rarely used in formal writing).
• Unlike conjunctions of addition (それに, そして): それとも does not add information but presents a choice.
• Can be used in indirect questions (…のか) to present two possibilities to be decided between.
fields.notes:
• In a long sentence, you can use two か particles around それとも: Aか、それともBか。
• Do not put それとも between two declarative clauses to express “or”; in that case use または/あるいは/か.
• それとも at the beginning of a sentence to “redirect” the question is also natural: それとも予定を変えますか？
• In fast conversation, a subject/predicate that is clear from context can be omitted. explain: Used to link two questions in order to offer the other person several choices ⏐ examples: 1. コーヒーにしますか。それとも紅茶にしますか。
Will you have coffee? Or tea?
2. 来週にしましょうか。それとも再来週がいいですか。
Shall we make it next week? Or would the week after be better?
3. 話し合って決めましょうか。それとも私が決めてしまってもいいですか。
Shall we talk it over and decide? Or is it all right if I just decide?
mistakes: Using それとも in a declarative sentence: pragmatically incorrect. Use または／あるいは／もしくは／AかBか instead.
Mixing “AかB、それともC？” is redundant; use “AかBか、それともC？” or rephrase the list to keep it balanced.
Leaving out the question mark at the end makes it an ambiguous statement; in exams there should be “？” or か at the end of the sentence.
Confusing it with それに/それから (adding information/continuing) → these do not express a choice.

fields.meaning: Is… (the formal polite form of です)
examples: This is our new product.
Thank you for calling. This is ABC Company.
The meeting room is on the 3rd floor.

fields.meaning: There is… (the formal polite form of あります)
examples: If you have any questions, please let us know.
The restroom is over there.
We apologize. All seats are currently taken.

fields.meaning: Be/come/go (honorific language (sonkeigo) for いる/来る/行く)
examples: The teacher is in the classroom now.
The company president is going to Osaka tomorrow.
Is Mr. Tanaka there?

fields.meaning: Do… (humble language (kenjōgo) for します)
examples: I will send you the materials.
I will contact you later.
Thank you in advance for your help.

fields.meaning: Do… (honorific language (sonkeigo) for する)
examples: The company president goes jogging every morning.
What do you do on weekends?

fields.name: お～になる（honorific）
fields.meaning: お+Vます+になる: do… (honorific language (sonkeigo))
examples: The company president has already gone home.
Have you read this book?

fields.meaning: While… (something happens at one point within a period)
fields.connection: V plain form + 間に / N + の / Na / Aい
examples: I'll go to the bank during my lunch break.

fields.meaning: Just by…, with only…

examples: Just looking at the picture made me want to eat that dish.

fields.meaning: Need…, … is necessary (Nが必要)
examples: You need a visa to work in Japan.

fields.meaning: Need to…, it is necessary to… (Vる必要がある)
examples: I need to submit the report by tomorrow.

fields.meaning: Made from… (raw material: から / visible material: で)
examples: Tofu is made from soybeans.
Sake is made from rice.

fields.meaning: Suddenly, all of a sudden…
examples: It suddenly started to rain.
The car stopped suddenly.

fields.meaning: Or…, or else… (choosing A or B)
examples: Please contact us by phone or email.
Please write with a pen or a pencil.

fields.meaning: Realize…, notice…
fields.connection: V plain form + こと + に気がつく に気がついた / N
examples: I realized I had left my umbrella on the train.

fields.name: Transitive verb・Intransitive verb（corresponding pairs）

examples: The window opened because of the wind.

fields.meaning: The particle て/で linking clauses: because A, B; A and then B
examples: In the morning I get up, take a shower, and go to school.

fields.meaning: Was doing… (past progressive ～ていた)
examples: Around 10 o'clock last night, I was taking a bath.

examples: Sorry I'm late.

fields.meaning: Glad that…, it was good that…
examples: I'm glad I got to meet you.

examples: His Japanese is so good that you could almost say he's Japanese.

fields.meaning: (I) heard that…, I was told that…
examples: I heard that Mr. Tanaka is going back to his country next month.

examples: I eat meat, but I don't eat fish.

fields.explain: Emphasizes comparison, contrast, or the speaker's volition or viewpoint.
fields.notes: meaning_vi: Contrast: A is…, while B is… (～は～が、～は～)

fields.meaning: Just as expected of…, living up to expectations (さすが)
fields.connection: さすが(に) + [sentence/clause] / さすがの + N + も
examples: That's a pro for you. You work so fast.
No wonder it's the most popular restaurant in Japan. It's delicious.
Even Mr. Tanaka couldn't solve this problem.

fields.name: お～する（humble）
fields.meaning: Do… (humble language (kenjōgo): おVますする/ごNする)
examples: Shall I carry your bag for you?
I'll show you the way to the station.
I borrowed a dictionary from my teacher.

fields.meaning: All the time, continuously (lasting without interruption over a period)
examples: It has been raining since this morning.
Yesterday I stayed home all day long.
I was waiting for him the whole time.

fields.meaning: Thank you for… (for me)
examples: Thanks for helping me.
Thanks for remembering my birthday.
Thanks for coming all the way to the station to pick me up.

fields.meaning: Rapidly, more and more…
examples: Your Japanese is getting better and better.
Prices keep going up and up.
If you have any questions, feel free to ask.

fields.meaning: Because… not… (reason; the second clause expresses an emotion/state)
fields.connection: Vなくて / Aくなくて / Naで(は)なくて / Nで(は)なくて + [sentence/clause]
examples: I didn't understand Japanese, so I was in trouble.
The bus didn't come, so I ended up being late.
It's a shame I couldn't pass the exam.

fields.meaning: A soft lead-in before a request/question (…, you see, the thing is…)
examples: There's something I'd like to ask you. Do you have a moment now?
About next week's meeting — is it OK if we change the time?
My computer won't work. Could you take a look at it?

fields.meaning: What if you ~? Why don't you try ~?
examples: If you're worried, why don't you call and ask?
You don't look well. Why don't you rest a bit?
fields.explain: ◎ A spoken language sentence pattern used when making a suggestion or an invitation. Just 「たら?」 is a casual way of speaking between equals.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: A way of advising the other person to do something.
examples: 1. ①　かさを　持って行ったらどう？
Why don't you take an umbrella?
2. ②　寒いでしょう。上着　着たら？
You're cold, aren't you? Why don't you put on a jacket?
3. ③　そろそろ　ねたらどう？
Why don't you go to bed soon?
4. ④　大丈夫ですか。少し　休んだらどうですか。
Are you OK? Why don't you rest a little?

fields.meaning: Even if… still
fields.connection: もし + Vても/Aくても/N・Naでも + [sentence/clause]
examples: Even if it rains, the match will be held as scheduled.
Even if I'm busy, I study Japanese for 10 minutes a day.
Even without money, you can live happily.
Even if he doesn't come, I'll start first.
Even if you're a student, you can take part in this event.
Even if the results are bad, let's keep going and not give up.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to affirm that the stance/volition in the second clause is not governed by the condition in the first clause.
Suitable for both spoken language and written language; “もし” makes the sentence clearer and more polite.
The second clause can be a command/advice/volition: ～してください／～しよう／～しなさい.
Do not use “もし” with self-evident conditions (universal truths) — in that case use plain ～ても.
Emphasize the degree with たとえ: たとえ失敗しても (even if I fail).

• Main meaning: “Even if ..., ...”. Presents a hypothetical condition (usually unfavorable or contrary to expectations), but the result in the second clause does not change.
• “もし” emphasizes the supposition; “もし” can be omitted when the context is clear.
• Nuance: concessive (concession). The second clause is usually the speaker's conclusion, volition, position, or evaluation, unaffected by the condition in the first clause.
• Degree of supposition: “もし～ても” is less extreme in nuance than “たとえ～ても” and stronger than bare “～ても”.
• Can be used with both present/future; can be accompanied by adverbs of emphasis: たとえ, いくら, どんなに, たとえ何回…ても.
fields.notes:
• Placing “もし” before a ～ても clause helps the listener recognize early that this is a supposition; useful in long sentences.
• In conversation, “もし～なら” often competes with “もし～ても” depending on the intention: a pure condition (なら) or a concession (ても).
• The second clause should be content that does “not depend” on the first clause; avoid naturally inevitable results (to avoid logical contradiction).
meaning_vi: A way of stating a hypothesis. Doing or not doing something even if the condition in the first clause is realized or met.
examples: 1. ①　苦しくても
Even if it's hard
2. ②　もし　連絡が　なくても　心配しないでください。
Even if you don't hear from me, please don't worry.
3. ③　明日　晴れても、せんたくを　しません。今日　全部　しましたから。
Even if it's sunny tomorrow, I won't do the laundry. That's because I did it all today.
4. ④　わたしが　いなくなっても、もう　大丈夫ですね。
You'll be fine now even without me, won't you?
mistakes: Confusing it with “なら”: もし雨なら中止だ (stating a condition) is different from もし雨が降っても行く (concession).
The second clause states a naturally inevitable consequence → does not make sense with ～ても (incorrect example: もし火をつけても燃える). Use と/ば for inevitability.
Forgetting to change い/な/N into the correct form: な・N must use でも, い-adjectives use ～くても.
JLPT: choose between たとえ～ても (strong) and もし～ても (neutral); pay attention to whether the context is emphatic.
